title: Professor Barnett, Theodore Brockhoven and the first Mardi Gras parade job
summary: A short lesson from a teaching family, then Brockhoven books Brown's band for the carnival parades with bands between floats.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Well, they used to have a professor, they used to teach music. I think his name was Barnett. He was a bass player. And the whole family played music. And we were at one time, we went over to that place to play for the old man. And I remember the old man being a teacher in legitimate music. It was just amazing to him to see how he played so well without using notes, you know what I mean? And everything from memory and completely dependent upon the air. To him, that was quite a sensation. And Brookhoven, I remember three-year-old Brookhoven. I did. I went over to each place one time, and I took one lesson. Or two. Two. After he gave me one lesson, I figured I knew I'd know. I had the idea. He just showed me how to blow it, you know. And old man Brookhoven. Theodore Brookhoven was the one that gave me my first carnival job for the parades. Now I'm not talking about the first carnival job we played for the Garden District Club, but for the floats in between the, you know, the bands in between the floats. We had professional bands. No school bands as they are now. Like the Rex Parade?

Yeah, the big one we played, all the parades. And in those days, we didn't have school bands. All professional musicians, each band. And he'd go out of the state in Mississippi, in Alabama, in Georgia. And even as far as Florida, they'd get different bands to come in there and to play this parade, these parades behind each float, you know.
Between each one of those floats is a band.

Oh, it's all beautiful. And the bands would be playing, and it was a much finer carnival than they have today, in my estimation. How big a band? How big a band? Well, about ten pieces. Ten pieces. Ten to twelve pieces in each band. And depending upon what unit it was, some of these country units would maybe have twelve or fifteen. But Theodore Brookhoven, I think, would only pay them one lump sum for bands. They'd have to split that up among themselves. But the union would furnish as many bands as they could, out of their own organization. And then from there, they'd import a lot of bands. So I happened to see the other of Brookhoven down there, and I was nervous and I think, I talked to anybody. I told him I had a good band, and he signed me up. He evidently heard about us, you know. And so he gave me a job. He gave me the first carnival job to play. So, I had quite a lot of fun around New Orleans in my young days.
